An order list endpoint is slow, and the SQL log shows why: one query for the orders, then one per order for its lines, one per order for its payments, and one per customer. In a test with EF Core 10 and SQLite, a page of 50 orders took 111 commands. The fix in the pull request adds four
calls, and the log drops to a single command, plus a warning nobody reads. That one command returned 1,500 rows of 17 columns and tracked 730 entities, to build 50 summaries of four values each.
The belief: N+1 is a missing-
problem. Include every navigation the code touches, and data access is fixed.
There's a lot of truth in it.

really does remove the extra round trips, and Microsoft's own performance guide says to load related entities eagerly when you know you'll need them. The number most people watch, queries per request, goes from 111 to 1. And on a development database with three orders, the new query is fast.
The catch: the number of queries is only one cost. The other is what each query brings back.

The extra queries appear whenever related data is loaded per row. With lazy loading proxies, every first access to a navigation runs its own query. In the test, mapping 50 orders to summaries ran 1 query for the orders, 50 for lines, 50 for payments and 10 for customers, one per distinct customer, since the change tracker reused customers it had already loaded. A
per item does the same thing. Microsoft's docs warn that lazy loading makes N+1 very easy to trigger and recommend avoiding it.

tells EF Core to bring whole entities for each navigation: every mapped column, tracked by default. The list page needed an order id, a customer name, a total and a payment count. The included query in the test returned 17 columns, including a 500-character product description that the page never shows, and left 730 entities in the change tracker.
When a single SQL query joins a parent to two collections at the same level, the database returns every combination: each line paired with each payment. That's a
. Ten lines and three payments make 30 rows per order, so 50 orders came back as 1,500 rows. EF Core knows this is risky: it logs
whenever a query loads more than one collection without a configured splitting behavior.
A projection asks for the answer
describes the result instead of the entities. EF Core translates the whole shape, including
over collections, into SQL, so the database computes the totals and returns one row per order. In the test, the projected query returned 50 rows of 4 columns and tracked nothing.
has no role here: in the test, adding it to a query that projects into a DTO changed nothing in the SQL.

content.text: Each split query is a separate statement. If another transaction changes the data between them, the parts can disagree; Microsoft's docs suggest a serializable or snapshot transaction when that matters. Every split also costs a round trip. Before EF Core 10, split queries with
needed a fully unique ordering to avoid returning wrong data; EF Core 10 makes the ordering consistent across the split queries.

on the context options. Every query that loads several collections without choosing
then throws, and the stack trace points at it.
